headlines.article_text: OpenAI’s Sachin Katti to leave infrastructure role, stay on as advisor Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Sachin Katti, OpenAI's infrastructure and compute lead, announced he is departing his role and will continue supporting the company as an advisor. Uday Ruddarraju, OpenAI's CTO of compute, will replace Katti and lead the company's overall compute organization, according to a spokesperson. Katti said in a post on LinkedIn that he "decided to move on to build something new." In an aerial view, the Stargate Oracle AI data center campus is seen on August 26, 2026 in Abilene, Texas. Brandon Bell | Getty Images OpenAI's infrastructure lead, Sachin Katti, announced on Wednesday that he is departing his role after roughly a year at the artificial intelligence company. Katti said in a post on LinkedIn that he "decided to move on to build something new," and he'll continue to support OpenAI as an advisor after his last day on Nov. 15. Uday Ruddarraju, who has been serving as OpenAI's CTO of compute, will replace Katti and lead the company's overall compute organization, according to a spokesperson. "Building AI infrastructure at this scale has given me an incredible view into every dimension of the compute world, from silicon and systems to datacenters, energy, supply chains, financing, and the economics of AI," Katti wrote. "I'm enormously proud of what our teams accomplished together and grateful to the partners who helped make it possible." OpenAI's compute organization is crucial to its overall strategy; it's tasked with developing the company's infrastructure roadmap and ensuring that it can train and serve its models. OpenAI is targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and it's involved with massive, multi-billion-dollar data center projects in states like Ohio , Texas and Georgia . The latest leadership shakeup lands during a tense moment for AI infrastructure in the U.S., where backlash against data centers has mounted over concerns about noise, electricity rates and water consumption. The issue has become a flashpoint in the upcoming midterm elections, where both Republican and Democratic candidates have campaigned against the facilities. "I'm proud of what we've built and have total confidence in Uday and the team to carry it forward," Katti said in a statement. "I'm a builder at heart, and I'm looking forward to building something new." Ruddarraju joined OpenAI in July of last year, according to his LinkedIn. He previously served as the head of infrastructure engineering at Elon Musk's xAI, which was acquired by SpaceX earlier this year. Katti's exit is the latest in a string of executive departures at OpenAI this year. In July, Fidji Simo , OpenAI's product and business chief, said she would move into an advisory role to focus on recovery after a "severe exacerbation of a chronic illness." The following month, Brad Lightcap , a longtime OpenAI executive, and Denise Dresser , who served as revenue chief, also left the company. OpenAI President Greg Brockman told CNBC at the time that he doesn't believe the wave of departures is atypical for a young company. He said since OpenAI is in the spotlight, "every departure gets scrutinized in a way that it doesn't otherwise." "There have been different eras where we have different sets of, of leaders in place," Brockman said. "I'm a constant, Sam [Altman] is a constant, and I think that we are stronger because of that resilience and diversity." Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 16%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said. "The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back." Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya , founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090, called out CoreWeave's soaring yields on X late Tuesday. That prompted Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to respond, "yikes." Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of his deep dive into whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk." 'Relatively bad' balance sheet CoreWeave's balance sheet is "relatively bad" compared to its neocloud peers, said Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. That's because CoreWeave has done more borrowing and is currently building more data centers, he explained. "The yields have blown out because there's just more and more concern — that I don't share — about the wherewithal of these guys [being] able to over time pay back their interest expense," Meeks said. "It's definitely not a deteriorating situation," he added. "Maybe it's not improving, and I didn't really expect it to improve until these data centers get up and running." He expects the company to report flat margins from June to September and guide for margins to have a pretty significant improvement between September and December. CoreWeave's next quarterly results are expected in November. Tech sector hit CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. The overall tech sector brought down the stock market on Wednesday with the Nasdaq Composite losing 1.4%. headlines.article_text: Bank of America (BAC) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Bank of America's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Revenue was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading. Misses in fixed income and equities trading revenue totaled roughly $750 million. The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%. In this article BAC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 5:33 05:33 Bank of America CEO on $1.2 billion fine: We're on the right course to remediate everything Squawk on the Street Bank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected. Shares of the bank fell as much as 8% in morning trading. Here's what the company reported: Earnings per share: 91 cents, may not compare with $1.10 expected by LSEG Revenue: $30.12 billion vs. $30.69 billion expected by LSEG The bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share. Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations. Fixed income trading revenue dropped 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate. Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million. The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%. Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance. Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate. 'Worst in class' In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter. The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, sparked questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets. On the company's earnings call Wednesday, several analysts remarked on the sharp decline in Bank of America shares and pressed Moynihan about earlier guidance that compliance costs would be contained. "Clearly you've had a huge charge this morning," JPMorgan analyst Vivek Juneja said. "It's not that you can't absorb a billion. … But obviously it's a reputational and confidence issue." Other analysts questioned management on the pace of future share repurchases and asked about the bank's underperformance in trading. Management blamed the firm's bond trading results on the sharp rise in interest rates during the period. "It just happens when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for" credit and mortgage trading businesses, CFO Alastair Borthwick said. 'The right course' Later Wednesday in an interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker , Moynihan didn't commit to a timeline on the resolution of regulatory issues. "We got to do the work, and then the regulators look at it," Moynihan said. "So I don't want to speculate about the precise timeline." The CEO added that he was "confident that we are on the right course to remediate everything." Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, added 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years. De opdracht volgt op het substantiële contract voor de installatie van funderingen, dat DEME in juli 2026 verwierf, en breidt de betrokkenheid van het bedrijf bij Zeevonk verder uit. Het windpark, een gezamenlijk project van Vattenfall en Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) via zijn Energy Investment Fund I, zal een totaal geïnstalleerd vermogen hebben van ongeveer 1 GW.
